name: Columns and Capital from Amman Jordan

facts.text: Limestone column and capital in three pieces, at least 2,000 years old, excavated near Amman, Jordan.
Amman was called Philadelphia in Roman times.
Bicentennial gift to the City of Philadelphia through the Penn Museum from Jordan's ambassador.
Stands on the green along Smith Walk between 33rd and 34th streets.
Three-story painted brick dwelling in the Italian Villa style at the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard.
Features an off-center square tower, a slate gable roof and a bay window.
A porch was added in 1901.
Served as an officer's residence until June 1960.
Designed by Irwin T. Catharine and built in 1922 to 1924 in the Colonial Revival style.
Named for D. Newlin Fell, a Pennsylvania Supreme Court justice from 1894 and chief justice until 1915.
Shares a site with the George C. Thomas Junior High School.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.
Designed by Irwin T. Catharine and built in 1935 to 1937 in the Art Deco style.
Three-story, 16-bay yellow brick building.
Named for Quaker iron ore manufacturer Delaplaine McDaniel (1817 to 1885), who left funds for the school.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1986.

name: Discovery Center at East Park Reservoir

facts.text: The East Park Reservoir opened in 1889 to supply clean water to Philadelphia.
In 1970 the Water Department stopped using the west basin and fenced off 50 acres of parkland.
Opened its gates on September 28, 2018, with the reservoir kept as a wildlife sanctuary.
Built in 1893 to 1894 and designed by architect Wilson Eyre.
Built as the home of Joseph Leidy Jr., nephew of the paleontologist Joseph Leidy.
Served as the clubhouse of the Poor Richard Club, an advertising group, from 1925 to 1979.
Now the headquarters of District 1199C, a hospital and health care workers union.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1980.

name: Edgar Allan Poe National Historic Site

facts.text: Only surviving Philadelphia house of the several where Poe lived between 1838 and 1844.
Poe rented the house in early 1843 with his wife Virginia and his mother-in-law Maria Clemm.
Rooms are left in arrested decay and are not furnished to look as they did in Poe's time.
The National Park Service took over the property in 1978 and reopened it to the public in 1980.
Built in 1853 to 1854 for brewer William Gaul, designed by architect Stephen D. Button in the Italianate style.
Actor Edwin Forrest bought it a year after completion and lived there until his death in 1872.
Housed the Philadelphia School of Design for Women from 1880 until 1960.
Home of the Freedom Theatre, which teaches acting and live theatre production.
Designated a National Historic Landmark in 1993.
Designed by Irwin T. Catharine and built in 1925 to 1926 in the Art Deco style.
Entrance has a portico with Doric columns and terra cotta colored tiles.
Named for Edwin M. Stanton, who was Secretary of War under Abraham Lincoln.
Located within the Christian Street Historic District and listed on the National Register in 1988.
Built in 1925 to 1926 in the Late Gothic Revival style.
Designed by Irwin T. Catharine.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.
Designed by Irwin T. Catharine and built in 1923 to 1924 in the Colonial Revival style.
Three-story, nine-bay brick building on a raised basement.
A $2.1 million playground with a basketball court and running track opened in November 2023.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.

name: First Bank of the United States

facts.text: The bank's Philadelphia branch opened on December 12, 1791, first operating from Carpenters' Hall.
Architect James Hoban is credited alongside Samuel Blodgett for the building.
Stephen Girard bought the building after the bank's charter expired in 1811 and opened his own bank there.
Stands within Independence National Historical Park.
Built in 1889 as a three-story, eight-bay brick building on a limestone base in the Late Victorian style.
Named for lawyer and amateur poet Francis Scott Key (1779 to 1843).
Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1986.
Built in 1916 and designed by William Steele & Sons for General Electric, which made electric switchboards there.
Reinforced concrete building with brick facing, at 421 North 7th Street in Callowhill.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1985.
Part of the former plant was converted into a concert venue that opened in 1995.
Created in 1934 by sculptor Albert Laessle and sited at Logan Square at 19th Street.
Bronze sculpture on a limestone base, 10 feet 8 inches tall.
Charles Grafly developed the concept, and his student Laessle completed it.
Commissioned by the State of Pennsylvania and the Pennypacker Memorial Commission.
Honors a Chester County native who became the youngest general of the Civil War at age 22.
Designed by Irwin T. Catharine and built in 1925 to 1926 in the Art Deco style.
Named for Civil War General John F. Reynolds (1820 to 1863).
Entrance has Doric columns and decorative terra cotta panels.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.
Honors Geoff Geppert of the Class of 2015, a Haverford College men's lacrosse captain.
Geppert, a native of Cleveland Heights, Ohio, died unexpectedly in fall 2017.
Dedicated by Haverford in a ceremony on Saturday, April 27, 2019.
Designed by Henry deCourcy Richards and built in 1906 to 1908 in the Colonial Revival style.
Three-story, seven-bay brick building in the Whitman neighborhood.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.
Designed by Irwin T. Catharine and built in 1924 to 1925 in the Art Deco style.
Four-story, nine-bay brick building on a raised basement.
Entrance portico has Doric columns, with a brick parapet at the roofline.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.
Also called the Livezey House; built around 1725 by Thomas Shoemaker.
Sold in 1747 to Thomas Livezey Jr., who built a mill on the site.
Livezey descendants lived there for more than 120 years.
The City bought the property in 1873 for Fairmount Park and the mill stopped operating.
Designated on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places on June 26, 1956.
Built between 1698 and 1700, the oldest church in Pennsylvania.
Congregation began on Tinicum Island in 1646 and moved to this site in 1677.
Swedish Lutheran at first, it has been Episcopalian since 1845.
Site of the first regular Lutheran ordination in the Americas, Justus Falckner's in 1703.
Designated a National Historic Site in 1942 and affiliated with Independence National Historical Park.
Bronze statue by sculptor John Massey Rhind, installed in 1900.
Shows Houston with his hand resting on an Irish wolfhound.
Placed by the Fairmount Park Commission to recognize Houston's donation of nearby land to the park.
Stands on a granite base off Harvey Street near Lincoln Drive.
Built between 1931 and 1935 as the main post office, a steel frame building clad in limestone.
Designed by the architects Rankin & Kellogg.
Measures 386 feet wide by 455 feet long.
Served as Philadelphia's main postal processing facility from 1933 until 2008.
